one_liner: A number that predicts how much reward an agent will get from any situation.
everyday: Imagine you're playing a game where you collect points. At any moment in the game, you could ask: if I continue playing from where I am right now, how many total points should I expect to get by the end? That expected total is the value of your current situation. The value function is the method you use to answer that question for any position you might find yourself in.

Why does this matter? Because when you're deciding what to do next, you want to pick actions that move you toward high-value situations. If you know that a certain move puts you in a situation worth 50 future points, and another move puts you in a situation worth 10 future points, you should pick the first one. The value function lets you compare positions before you actually play them out.

There's a catch: future rewards are uncertain. You might make a great move, but then get unlucky and lose points. The value function handles this by calculating the average or expected total reward, not a guarantee. It's like asking: if I did this move thousands of times, what would be my typical outcome? That typical outcome is what the formula computes.
symbols: the value of a state — the expected total reward you'll get if you're in situation s and act optimally from now on
a state or situation — any snapshot of where you are in the game or problem (position, inventory, current observation, etc.)
the expected value or average — if you played this out many times, what's the typical total?
time step or turn — how many moves ahead into the future

gamma, the discount factor — a number between 0 and 1 that says how much we care about future rewards compared to immediate rewards (closer to 1 means future matters almost as much; closer to 0 means only immediate rewards matter)
the reward received at time step t — the points or signal you get right now
sum or add up — combine all the discounted rewards over all future time steps

worked.title: Finding the value of a position in a simple game
lines: Suppose you're in a state where: immediate reward is 10 points, discount is γ=0.9,
and the next state gives 5 points, the one after gives 2 points, then game ends.
So V(s) = 16.12: from this position, you expect to earn 16.12 points on average.

matters: The value function appears in nearly every method that makes a learning agent: reinforcement learning agents use it to pick actions, language models use it to evaluate which tokens (the individual words or word-pieces it generates) are good choices, robots use it to plan movements, and systems that learn from human feedback use it to measure progress. Anywhere a decision-maker must choose between options, the value function answers the core question: which choice leads to better outcomes down the line, because it measures the total reward each option produces.

The formula works because it converts the vague idea of future reward into a single number you can compare and optimize. Instead of running every possible sequence of moves to see which is best (impossible for complex problems), the value function learns a shortcut: given any situation, instantly predict the expected future reward. This lets agents make smart decisions fast, even in situations they've never seen before, because they understand the shape of what matters.
